title: Qvevri
subtitle: Buried clay vessels
objectives: Explain how qvevri wine is made

steps.title: Clay underground
steps.body: A qvevri is a large, egg-shaped clay vessel, from about 800 to several thousand litres, buried up to its neck in the ground. The inside is coated with beeswax. The earth keeps the temperature cool and stable, around 13 to 15 degrees, during fermentation and ageing. Qvevri are made by hand by a few master potters.

steps.title: The method
steps.body: Crushed grapes, often with skins, seeds and sometimes stems, chacha, go into the qvevri. Fermentation starts with native yeasts. The cap is punched down, then the qvevri is sealed with a stone or wooden lid and clay. The wine stays on the skins for months, often until spring. The egg shape helps solids settle at the bottom.

options: The earth keeps the temperature cool and stable

steps.title: UNESCO
steps.body: In 2013, UNESCO added the ancient Georgian traditional qvevri winemaking method to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The method inspired producers worldwide, especially in Friuli, where Josko Gravner began using qvevri in 2001, and in the natural wine movement.

steps.explanation: Qvevri winemaking uses clay, not oak.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Qvevri are egg-shaped clay vessels buried in the ground
Grapes ferment with skins for months
